prompt.context: Pharma+ has developed an ultra fast treatment for dyspepsia (heartburns and other mild abdominal pains). Take the pill and symptoms disappear within the hour. Pharma+'s CEO believes the new molecule is revolutionary.
prompt.question: The CEO wants your help to fix the price for this new drug. How would you approach pricing this new product?

clarifying_info.a: Clinical trials showed side effects limited to frequent migraine, so not to be advised for children. Results were similar for males and females.
It can be sold OTC, meaning the patient is the real customer.

clarifying_info.q: What is the efficacy compared to existing treatments?
clarifying_info.a: During clinical trials, 75% of patients stopped reporting symptoms using 2 pills per day.

Existing treatments (antacids, prokinetics, H2-blockers, PPIs) are popular but frustratingly low efficacy. In over 50% of patients, herbal products such as ginger or peppermint generally have as much anti-dyspeptic effect as best-in-class medications.
Competitor prices range from $15 to $50 for a one-month supply, with dosages of 2 to 3 pills per day.
R&D = $10m total; manufacturing (marginal cost) = $0.50 per pill; marketing and sales (effective cost per pill) = $0.50 per pill.

exhibits.title: Price Line ($/month)
exhibits.shows: A price line showing the spectrum from $15 to $100 per month with labeled zones for competition, costs, economic value to consumer, and no-demand territory.

framework: Product characteristics and target market: efficacy, side effects, OTC vs. Rx, who is the real customer
Market sizing: estimate number of dyspepsia sufferers in the US who are treatable
Competitor benchmarking: existing treatments, price range, efficacy comparison
Economic value to the consumer: willingness to pay, benchmarks beyond pharma (healthy diet spending, wellness)

questions.prompt: Define and size the total addressable US market for this drug.
questions.guidance: Candidate should segment the US population (320m) by age 20–80, apply prevalence rates and treatment-seeking rates per cohort. Strong answer shows awareness of differential prevalence (young professionals stress-induced, elderly daily-pill takers).

math.setup: US population ~320m; only 20–80 year-olds are relevant. Apply % affected and % treated per age band at 2 pills/day posology.
steps: At 2 pills/day × 30 days = 60 pills/month per patient
Total annual pills (if all on treatment): 40m × 60 × 12 = ~28.8 billion pills per year
math.answer: Approximately 40 million treatable patients in the US; total potential pill volume is ~28.8 billion pills/year.

questions.prompt: Based on costs, competition, and consumer value, what price per month would you recommend?
questions.guidance: Candidate should anchor pricing using three reference points: cost floor (~$1/pill = $60/month), competitive ceiling ($50/month top of range), and consumer willingness to pay benchmarks (e.g., healthy diet spend ~$100/month). A strong answer proposes ~$2/pill ($100/month) with a clear markup rationale and breakeven check.

math.setup: Cost per pill = $0.50 manufacturing + $0.50 marketing = $1.00 total variable cost. Proposed price = $2/pill. Monthly supply at 2 pills/day = 60 pills.
steps: Monthly cost to produce and market: 60 pills × $1.00 = $60/month
Breakeven on R&D ($10m): $10m ÷ $1 profit per pill = 10m pills, or ~167k patient-months, or ~14k patients taking it for 1 year
At 1% US market share: 40m × 1% = 400k patients × $60/month profit × 12 months = ~$288m/year profit
math.answer: Recommended price: $2/pill / ~$100/month supply (100% markup). Breakeven = 10m pills (~20k customers for 1 year). At 1% market share, ~$200–288m annual earnings.

brainstorming.prompt: What creative approaches or considerations could support a premium pricing strategy beyond standard pharmaceutical benchmarks?

categories.name: Value proposition extensions
ideas: Benchmark against wellness spending (healthy diet, gym memberships, supplements) rather than only pharma
Highlight speed of relief (within 1 hour) vs. slow-acting competitors
75% efficacy vs. competitors' near-herbal-equivalent efficacy is a major differentiator

categories.name: Customer segmentation
ideas: Young professionals willing to pay premium to stay productive
Elderly patients who already take daily pills and seek convenience
Corporate wellness programs as a bulk buyer channel

categories.name: Distribution and marketing
ideas: Pharmacy shelf placement and brand visibility

categories.name: Pricing structure options
ideas: Subscription/monthly auto-ship to lock in recurring revenue
Introductory price to build share then raise
Bundle with complementary GI wellness products

recommendation: Advertise the clinical trial results (75% efficacy, fast relief) to differentiate from current low-efficacy standard of care
Price at $2 per pill (~$100/month) targeting the high end of the competitive range and matching consumer willingness to pay for health/wellness products
risks: Migraine side effect may limit uptake among sensitive or headache-prone patients; label warning required
Competitors could respond with price cuts or accelerated product development
Consumer price sensitivity if insurance does not cover an OTC product
next_steps: Run breakeven and sensitivity analysis at different market penetration rates
Pilot marketing campaign emphasizing speed and efficacy to validate $100/month price point
Explore insurance coverage or employer-sponsored wellness program partnerships to broaden access
